title: Three threads of reinforcement learning
tagline: Trial-and-error learning came from animal psychology, optimal control from dynamical systems, and temporal-difference learning from prediction. Q-learning is where the three threads finally meet.

events.title: Bain: learning by “groping and experiment”
events.summary: Woodworth traces the idea of trial-and-error learning back to Alexander Bain’s discussion in the 1850s.

events.title: Lloyd Morgan names “trial and error”
events.summary: The British ethologist uses the term explicitly to describe what he observes in animal behaviour.

events.title: Thorndike’s Law of Effect
events.summary: Responses followed by satisfaction become more likely to recur; those followed by discomfort, less likely. This is the first succinct statement of the principle.

events.title: “Reinforcement” enters the vocabulary
events.summary: The word first appears in this context in the English translation of Pavlov’s monograph on conditioned reflexes.

events.title: Ross builds a maze-learning machine
events.summary: Possibly the earliest electro-mechanical learner: it finds its way through a simple maze and remembers the path in switch settings.

events.title: Turing’s “pleasure–pain system”
events.summary: A report sketches a machine that makes random choices where action is undetermined, cancelling them on pain and fixing them on pleasure.

events.title: Shannon: a program that improves its own evaluation
events.summary: Shannon suggests a computer could play chess with an evaluation function and improve by modifying that function online—the seed of Samuel’s method.

events.title: Walter’s tortoise and Shannon’s Theseus
events.summary: Grey Walter’s mechanical tortoise learns in a simple way; Shannon’s maze-running mouse finds its route by trial and error, with the maze itself remembering via magnets and relays.

events.title: Minsky’s SNARCs; Farley and Clark’s simulation
events.summary: Minsky describes an analog machine of Stochastic Neural-Analog Reinforcement Calculators. Farley and Clark simulate a network that learns by trial and error, while Deutsch describes a maze solver with model-based traits.

events.title: Minsky links secondary reinforcement to machines
events.summary: Minsky may have been the first to see that a stimulus paired with a primary reinforcer—the psychologist’s secondary reinforcer—matters for artificial learning systems.

events.title: Bellman: dynamic programming and MDPs
events.summary: Extending Hamilton and Jacobi, Bellman defines the value function and Bellman equation, then introduces the discrete stochastic case—Markov decision processes.

events.title: Samuel’s checkers player
events.summary: The first learning method to implement temporal-difference ideas, developed with no reference to Minsky or to animal learning.

events.title: Howard’s policy iteration
events.summary: A method for solving Markov decision processes that remains an essential element of modern reinforcement-learning theory.

events.title: Minsky’s “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence”
events.summary: Names the credit-assignment problem: how to distribute credit for success among the many decisions that produced it.

events.title: MENACE and STeLLA
events.summary: Michie’s matchbox engine learns tic-tac-toe with coloured beads. Andreae’s STeLLA learns by trial and error with an internal model of the world.

events.title: “Reinforcement learning” enters engineering
events.summary: Waltz and Fu—followed by Mendel, Fu, and others—use the terms for engineering applications of trial-and-error learning.

events.title: BOXES balances a pole
events.summary: Michie and Chambers apply their controller to a pole hinged on a cart, learning from a failure signal alone—the best early example of an RL task under incomplete knowledge.

events.title: Klopf revives the hedonic thread
events.summary: Klopf argues that the drive to get a result from the environment was being lost as research turned to supervised learning. His generalized reinforcement also brushed against temporal-difference ideas.

events.title: Learning with a critic; learning automata
events.summary: Widrow, Gupta, and Maitra modify LMS to learn from success and failure instead of examples. Work on learning automata and the k-armed bandit joins the thread.

events.title: Holland’s adaptive systems and classifier systems
events.summary: A general theory based on selectional principles later becomes classifier systems with a bucket-brigade credit-assignment algorithm close to temporal difference.

events.title: Witten publishes the first TD rule
events.summary: What we now call tabular TD(0), inside an adaptive controller for MDPs. The paper spans trial-and-error learning and optimal control while contributing to the third thread.

events.title: Sutton: learning driven by successive predictions
events.summary: Sutton develops Klopf’s ideas into learning rules driven by changes in temporally successive predictions, with links to animal learning theory.

events.title: A TD model of classical conditioning
events.summary: Sutton and Barto build a psychological model of classical conditioning on temporal-difference learning; other influential models follow through the decade.

events.title: The actor–critic architecture
events.summary: Barto, Sutton, and Anderson combine temporal-difference learning with trial-and-error learning and apply it to Michie and Chambers’ pole-balancing problem.

events.title: Werbos argues for interrelating DP and learning
events.summary: An explicit case for joining dynamic programming with learning methods, and for its relevance to neural and cognitive mechanisms.

events.title: TD(λ): prediction separated from control
events.summary: Sutton treats temporal-difference learning as a general prediction method, introduces TD(λ), and proves some of its convergence properties.

events.title: Watkins’s Q-learning unites the threads
events.summary: Q-learning extends and integrates prior work in all three threads. Watkins’s treatment of reinforcement learning in the MDP formalism has been widely adopted since.

events.title: TD-Gammon
events.summary: Tesauro combines the tic-tac-toe algorithm with a neural network on backgammon’s 10²⁰ states, beating every previous program and eventually the best human players.

events.title: Dopamine looks like a TD signal
events.summary: Researchers converge on an uncanny similarity between temporal-difference algorithms and the activity of dopamine-producing neurons, opening a subfield of neuroscience.

events.title: Neurodynamic programming
events.summary: Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis name the combination of dynamic programming and artificial neural networks, developing the relationship Watkins opened.

source.title: Early History of Reinforcement Learning
source.citation: Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd edition, §1.7
